newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan-S.Korea nuclear waste row escalates.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan-S.Korea nuclear waste row escalates.

text.p: A row over Taiwan's plan to ship nuclear waste to Stalinist North Korea escalated on Thursday, with supporters clashing with South Korean anti-nuclear activists and burning the visitors' protest banners.
The seven South Korean activists were later deported at 5.15 p.m. (0915 GMT), state television said. Police earlier said the group were being deported because they had breached Taiwan's assembly law.

Scores of Taiwanese led by Taipei county councillor Ching Chia-shou torched a banner held by the South Korean activists outside state utility Taiwan Power Co's headquarters in central Taipei, state television showed.
"They (the seven South Koreans) have violated the purpose of the visit stated in their visas, and we want to prevent further conflicts between them and local groups," a police official said.
Ching, a veteran champion of nationalist causes told Reuters: "We cannot tolerate the (South Koreans') action".
Ching was among Taiwan and Hong Kong activists who pierced a Japanese maritime cordon in October to hoist Nationalist and Communist Chinese flags on an East China Sea island also claimed by Tokyo.
"We were not afraid of hundreds of Japanese warships then and we are not afraid of the South Koreans now," Ching said.
Undaunted, the South Koreans used a professional mountain climber to hang a huge green banner reading "Stop exporting nuclear waste" from a 12-storey building across from Taiwan Power Co's office.
The move triggered a confrontation between the South Korean and Taiwan activists, but police promptly broke it up.
The police officer said one of the South Korean activists "was kicked a bit" during the confrontation, but added "it was not serious".
The South Koreans, who began a five-day hunger strike on Wednesday, took their complaints to North Korea's unofficial travel office in Taipei but were denied entrance.
China on Thursday slammed the Taiwan-North Korea nuclear waste deal, saying the scheme was a blatant attempt by Taipei to spoil Beijing's ties with its communist neighbour.
"China's government and people express their resolute opposition to the actions of the Taiwan authorities," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing in Beijing.
Taiwan's nuclear waste plan was a clear attack on Beijing's cherished goal of reunification with the Nationalist-ruled island, Shen said.
China has considered Taiwan a renegade province since a civil war in 1949 split them.

Despite the protests, Taiwan and North Korea have forged ahead with preparations for an initial shipment of 60,000 barrels of the waste, though nothing can move before permits are issued by Taiwan's Atomic Energy Commission.
South Korea, worried the deal could pollute the Korean peninsula with radioactivity, says there is no verification that the North -- Seoul's arch-rival -- can store the waste safely.
Taiwan maintains the Taipei-Pyongyang waste pact complies with all international regulations and that shipments would be securely packed in steel barrels.
The U.S. State Department said on Wednesday that any shipment of nuclear waste from Taiwan to North Korea should conform to international standards.
Taiwan has no diplomatic ties with either North Korea or South Korea, both of which recognise Taiwan's own rival -- the communist Chinese government in Beijing.
